figures.alt: Illustration of a calm Michigan lake at night under a crescent moon and stars, with pine trees along the shore.
figures.caption: The Moon and the stars show up at night. In the day the bright sky hides the stars.

figures.alt: Illustration of a father with a child on his shoulders and a grandmother in a park on a long summer evening with the sun still high.
figures.caption: In Michigan summer there is daylight late into the evening.

figures.alt: Illustration of a girl pulling a sled across a snowy park as a low orange sun sets behind bare trees.
figures.caption: In winter the Sun sets early, so there is less daylight.

figures.alt: Illustration of a paper plate with a straw standing in its center on a sunny sidewalk. The straw shadow falls across the plate, away from the Sun.
figures.caption: Paper-plate sundial: the shadow points away from the Sun, and it moves as the day goes on.

figures.alt: The Sun on the left shines on a round Earth. The half of Earth facing the Sun is bright and the other half is dark. A curved arrow shows Earth turning, so a place on the bright side turns into the dark side.
figures.caption: The Sun stays put and Earth spins. A place facing the Sun has day. When Earth turns that place away, it has night.

figures.alt: Two sky pictures side by side. Left, night: a dark sky with stars and a crescent Moon. Right, day: a bright blue sky with the Sun, no stars visible, and dashed circles where the stars still are.
figures.caption: The stars are still in the sky in the daytime. Stars are faraway suns, and the bright sky hides them.

figures.alt: Interactive: a slider turns a ball that stands for Earth in front of a lamp, and says whether your place, a red dot, is in day or night.
figures.caption: Turn the Earth and watch your place go from day to night. The Sun does not turn off: Earth turns.

figures.alt: Interactive: a slider changes the sky from bright day to dark night. Stars fade in as the sky darkens, and dashed rings show where they still are in daylight.
figures.caption: Darken the sky and the stars appear. They were there all day.

figures.alt: Bar graph, About how much daylight (squares of light). December 9 squares, March 12 squares, June 15 squares.
figures.caption: Michigan daylight strips, about 9 squares of light in December, 12 in March and 15 in June. Summer days have more daylight.
